edition.locus: Against Marcion 1.1 (Pontic barbarian; apostate from prior faith; novelty prescription)

source_text: Si quid retro gestum est nobis aduersus Marcionem. iam hinc uiderit. nouam rem adgredimur ex uetere. primum opusculum quasi properatum pleniore postea compositione rescideram. hanc quoque nondum exemplariis suffectam fraude tunc fratris, dehinc apostatae, amisi, qui forte descripserat quaedam mendosissime et exhibuit frequentiae. emendationis necessitas facta est innouationis. eius occasio aliquid adicere persuasit. ita stilus iste nunc de secundo tertius et de tertio iam hinc primus hunc opusculi sui exitum necessario praefatur, ne quem uarietas eius in disperso reperta confundat. Pontus igitur, qui Euxinus natura negatur, nomine inluditur. ceterum hospitalem Pontum nec de situ aestimes; ita ab humanioribus fretis nostris quasi quodam barbariae suae pudore secessit. gentes ferocissimae inhabitant; si tamen habitatur in plaustro. sedes incerta, uita cruda, libido promiscua et plurimum nuda; etiam cum abscondunt, suspensis de iugo pharetris ut indicibus notantur, ne qui intercedat. ita nec armis suis erubescunt. parentum cadauera cum pecudibus caesa conuiuio conuorant. qui non ita decesserint, ut escatiles iuerint, maledicta mors est. nec feminae sexu mitigantur secundum pudorem; ubera excludunt, pensum securibus faciunt, malunt militare quam nubere. duritia de caelo quoque. dies numquam patens, sol numquam ridens, unus aer nebula, totus annus hibernum, omne quod fiauerit aquilo est. liquores niuibus redeunt, amnes glacie negantur, montes pruina exaggerantur. omnia torpent, omnia rigent; nihil illic nisi feritas calet, illa scilicet, quae fabulas scaenis dedit de sacrificiis Taurorum et amoribus Colchorum et crucibus Caucasorum. sed nihil tam barbarum ac triste apud Pontum quam quod illic Marcion natus est, Scytha tetrior, Hamaxobio instabilior, Massageta inhumanior, Amazona audacior, nubilo obscurior, hieme frigidior, gelu fragilior, Histro fallacior, Caucaso abruptior. quidni? penes quem uerus Prometheus, deus omnipotens, blasphemiis lancinatur. iam et bestiis illius barbariei importunior Marcion. quis enim tam castrator carnis castor quam qui nuptias abstulit? quis tam comesor mus Ponticus quam qui euangelia conrosit? ne tu, Euxine, probabiliorem feram philosophis edidisti quam Christianis. nam ille canicola Diogenes hominem inuenire cupiebat. lucernam meridie circumferens, Marcion deum, quem inuenerat, extincto lumine fidei suae amisit. non negabunt discipuli eius primam illius fidem nobiscum fuisse, ipsius litteris testibus, ut hinc iam destinari possit haereticus qui deserto quod prius fuerat id postea sibi elegerit, quod retro non erat. in tantum enim haeresis deputabitur quod postea inducitur, in quantum ueritas habebitur quod retro et a primordio traditum est. sed alius libellus hunc gradum sustinebit aduersus haereticos, etiam sine retractatu doctrinarum reuincendos. quod hoc sint de praescriptione nouitatis. nunc quatenus admittenda congressio est interdum, ne compendium praescriptionis ubique aduocatum diffidentiae deputetur, regulam prius aduersarii praetexam, ne cui lateat, in qua principalis quaestio dimicatura est.
pass_a_gloss: Pontus Marcionem peiorem bestiis. Primam fidem nobiscum; haeresis = nouitas.
pass_b_english: Whatever was formerly done by us against Marcion—from here let it see to itself. We approach a new matter from an old. The first little work, as if hurried, I had afterward cut back by a fuller composition. This too, not yet furnished to copies, I lost by the fraud then of a brother, afterward an apostate, who by chance had copied some things most faultily and displayed them to a crowd. Necessity of correction became necessity of renewal. Its occasion persuaded to add something. So this pen, now third from the second and from the third already from here first, necessarily prefaces this outcome of its little work, lest the variety of it found scattered confuse anyone.

Pontus, then, which is denied to be Euxine by nature, is mocked by the name. For the rest, do not even judge Pontus hospitable from its site; so far has it withdrawn from our more human seas as if by a certain shame of its own barbarism. Most fierce nations dwell there—if yet one dwells in a wagon. Uncertain seats, crude life, promiscuous lust and for the most part naked; even when they hide, they are marked by quivers hung from the yoke as signs, lest anyone intervene. So they do not blush even at their own arms. Parents’ corpses, slaughtered with cattle, they devour at a feast. Whoever have not so departed as to have gone edible—that is a cursed death. Nor are women softened by sex according to modesty; they shut out the breasts, make their spinning with axes, prefer to soldier than to marry. Hardness from the sky too. Day never open, sun never laughing, one air mist, the whole year winter, everything that has blown is the north wind. Liquids return to snows, rivers are denied by ice, mountains are heaped with frost. All things stiffen, all things freeze; nothing there is hot except fierceness—that of course which gave the stages tales of the Taurians’ sacrifices and the Colchians’ loves and the Caucasus’ crosses.

But nothing so barbarous and grim at Pontus as that Marcion was born there—more frightful than a Scythian, more unstable than a wagon-dweller, more inhuman than a Massagete, bolder than an Amazon, darker than cloud, colder than winter, more brittle than frost, more treacherous than the Danube, more abrupt than Caucasus. Why not? With whom the true Prometheus, the almighty God, is mangled by blasphemies. Already Marcion is also more troublesome than that barbarism’s beasts. For who is so much a beaver, castrator of flesh, as he who took away marriages? Who so much a Pontic mouse, devourer, as he who has gnawed the gospels? Truly, Euxine, you have brought forth a beast more acceptable to philosophers than to Christians. For that dog Diogenes was wanting to find a human, carrying a lantern at noon; Marcion, with the light of his faith extinguished, lost the God he had found. His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, by his own letters as witnesses, so that from here already he can be marked a heretic who, having deserted what he had been before, afterward chose for himself what formerly was not. For so far will that be counted heresy which is afterward introduced, inasmuch as that will be held truth which was handed down formerly and from the beginning. But another booklet will sustain this step against heretics, to be refuted even without rehandling of doctrines, because they are this by prescription of novelty. Now, inasmuch as a contest is sometimes to be admitted, lest the shortcut of prescription everywhere invoked be counted as diffidence, I will first string out the adversary’s rule, lest it be hidden from anyone, in which the principal question is going to fight.

choices.choice: mark Marcion heretic by deserting prior shared faith for later novelty
rejected: treat his later stranger-god as original apostolic deposit

choices.choice: hold truth as what was handed from the beginning against post-introduced heresy
rejected: equate gospel-gnawing novelty with the ancient rule
